content: Renaissance Wax is a wax polish that is extensively utilized in the fields of antique restoration and museum curation. While it is not suitable for all materials, it is widely recognized and employed by nearly every collection. Additionally, it serves as a primary finishing agent for cabinetry and furniture. According to a typical commercial supplier of conservation materials, Renaissance Wax is used to rejuvenate and protect valuable items such as furniture, leather, paintings, metals, marble, onyx, and ivory. It enhances colors and imparts a soft sheen to treated surfaces. In conservation practices, wax coatings are most commonly and least controversially applied to metals. The application of wax on metals serves several purposes: it creates a barrier that prevents moisture and oxygen from reaching the metal surface, protects against the introduction of contaminants through handling, and provides a protective layer over anti-corrosion undercoatings. However, waxes should not be applied to materials with intentionally loose or powdery surfaces. The wax is applied evenly and lightly across the surface, followed by gentle buffing with a smooth, lint-free cloth to achieve a sheen. For items with intricate shapes, a brush may be used instead. The application technique and tools must be tailored to the specific requirements of the item being treated. In the conservation of leather bookbindings affected by red rot, it is common practice to first consolidate the leather using Klucel G or a similar consolidant, followed by the application of a protective coating of Renaissance Wax. Similarly, in the conservation of metals, an undercoat such as Incralac may be applied first, with Renaissance Wax layered on top. Renaissance Wax was originally developed in the early 1950s by the research laboratories of the British Museum. It is now exclusively manufactured by Picreator Enterprises Ltd. Earlier wax polishes, which were based on beeswax and carnauba wax, either contained acids or became acidic over time. In contrast, Renaissance Wax is formulated using more stable microcrystalline waxes refined from crude oil. It also contains polyethylene waxes, such as Cosmolloid 80H, which are absent in some other formulations. The preparation involves melting the waxes together, pouring them into 300 ml of a high flash point hydrocarbon solvent, and stirring continuously until cool. A harder coating can be achieved by modifying the formulation, adding white spirit to adjust the consistency. Despite its widespread use and general acceptance as a stable and effective material for conservation work, Renaissance Wax is not without its critics. Wax coatings are known to attract dust and lint, and they may obscure fine details on the surface of objects. Furthermore, some authors have reported difficulties in removing Renaissance Wax, likely due to its polyethylene wax content.
